text: Hi, Katie. Welcome to This is My Architecture.
Would you please briefly talk about TXCraft?
Yeah, TXCraft is now the number one ticketing system in Taiwan.
And we sell tickets for sports events, film festivals, and mainly for concerts.
And you know, every time we sell tickets for concerts, there will be lots of people coming,
trying to grab a ticket they want.
So, you know, we're not like the average web that faces a smooth curve like traffic,
but we have to face a peak, a very huge peak when we sell tickets every week.
So that's a problem we have, and that's a problem we have to solve.
Right. So, TXCraft is an online ticket selling website, which is designed for handling millions of concurrent users.
Yes.

Okay. Now you can see it's a simplified architecture of our system.
And every time when the fans come, they will come to EOP first.
And then we will pass the traffic to EC2 instances.
And EC2 instances will pass the request to our DynamoDB.
And then we have a second group of API interface that we will handle everything from DynamoDB to our EC2 servers,
and pass the result back to DynamoDB.
That is our architecture.
Right. So we have two groups of EC2 instances here.
One group is for the UI layer, and the other group is for the API layer.
Yes.
So how do you prepare the EC2 instances to handle the spiky traffic?
How does the auto-scaling work here?
Okay. Since we have sold lots of tickets many times,
so we have to estimate how many people will come up to our website to have the tickets,
to try to purchase the tickets.
So when we have that estimated number,
we will provision our ELB, provision our EC2 instances.
And mostly we will prepare for spot instances, maybe 80 to 90 percent of it.
And if we want to keep the persistency of our spot instances,
we will use the spot block to protect our spot instances for one hour.

Right. So let's talk about the database layer, which is using the DynamoDB.

and then we will keep the numbers down to the original normal ones.
